---
title: "Why Rust"
subtitle: "What a Rust core buys, what it costs, and what the measurements say so far."
---

## What it buys

**One implementation for two languages.** The Python package is a thin wrapper around
the Rust crates (pyo3, built with maturin). There is no second implementation to keep
in step: the parity suite asserts that Python returns the same bits as Rust on shared
inputs for every task, and the release examples print the same results in both
languages ([Get started](get-started.qmd)).

**Memory behaviour you can see.** The Rust benchmark driver counts every allocation
per phase. That is how the repository found that the forest port makes 580k to 2.0M
allocations per fit where a linear fit makes a few hundred, and recorded it as the
first optimisation target instead of a claim.

**Speed where R pays for orchestration.** On the framework-overhead tasks, where both
sides run the same algorithm (`lm`, `glm`, rpart, xgboost versus their ports), the
measured differences are large and fall with the number of rows: per cold workflow fit
the native ports are 3.4–930× faster than R tidymodels for linear and logistic models
(OLS 930× at 342 rows, 12× at 100k, 6.1× at 1e6; logistic 3.4× at 1e6), 14–270× for
rpart-style trees, 1.9–4.4× for xgboost-style boosting; 10-fold cross-validation
3.7–2200× (linear / logistic), 13–470× (trees), 2.6–7.8× (boosting); workflow sets
14–270×. R's peak memory is 3.1–70× the Rust binary's. All of it on one Windows laptop
with R single-threaded on reference BLAS, at one thread unless stated; the ranges are
recomputed from the per-trial CSVs on every site build and their caveats are on the
[Benchmarks](benchmarks.qmd) page.

**A port can be checked.** Because the semantics are ported from the installed R
package sources rather than re-invented, every ported behaviour has an R reference to
test against. The differential suite does that per quantity, and the tolerance file
records every bound with its measurement ([Verification](verification.qmd)).

## What it costs

**No R interface.** This is a Rust library with a Python wrapper; R users keep
tidymodels. The project is not a replacement for it and does not try to be.

**A smaller ecosystem.** tidymodels is a family of packages. This project covers parts
of recipes, parsnip, rsample, yardstick, tune, workflows and workflowsets and nothing of
the rest; the [Gaps](gaps.qmd) page keeps the list.

**A port is not the original.** Two findings on record show what that means in
practice:

- The random-forest port follows ranger's growing rules but draws from its own random
  number generator, so a forest is never R's forest; it is verified statistically (4
  standard-error bands over 10 seeds on each side), and in the benchmarks it is **on
  par with ranger** (0.86–1.04× per fit), not faster.
- The xgboost port mirrors xgboost's float32 arithmetic and is bit-exact against R's
  xgboost on Windows, where the fixtures were made. On Linux and macOS the C runtime's
  `expf` rounds differently in the last ulp, and that ulp shows up in the fold boosters'
  statistics; the tolerance file carries measured per-platform bounds for exactly those
  quantities (ADR-0017) rather than a loosened default.

**Different optimizers, different numbers.** Where the port uses a different algorithm
from R (the penalised logistic path against glmnet), the benchmark is reported in its
own category and the comparison is never described as like for like.

## What is not measured

A second benchmark platform (the CI runners are not benchmark machines), parity of the
xgboost port against an xgboost built on Linux or macOS, and an independent review of
the verification record are open items in the repository's roadmap
([Roadmap](roadmap.qmd)).
